title: Backbone girders are shallower than engineers would build because flexibility is needed

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Backbone girders are shallower than engineers would build because flexibility is needed

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The vertebral girder of large animals such as Diplodocus or Stegosaurus is shallower than an engineer's cantilever of comparable load, because a deeper girder would increase rigidity, and an animal's backbone must combine strength with flexibility.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: If we adopt a much greater depth (or ratio of depth to length) as in the modern cantilever, we shall greatly increase the _strength_ of the structure; but at the same time we should greatly increase its _rigidity_, and this is precisely what, in the circumstances of the case, it would seem that nature is bound to avoid.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVI, “On Form and Mechanical Efficiency”; topic “Strength versus flexibility of the backbone”. Scope: vertebral columns of large vertebrates

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch16-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.49

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A Pareto analysis captures the intended trade-off, but “shallower than an engineer would build” lacks a fixed design specification. Existing morphology permits illustrative tests, not a decisive test of the causal necessity.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare vertebral depth-to-length ratios with optimized cantilever designs under estimated loads, then model the strength-flexibility Pareto frontier and locate observed skeletons on it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No unique engineer's comparator is specified.

Required flexibility and safety factors are unknown, especially for fossils.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Depth-to-length of a backbone is measurable on open scans, including some of the large animals named in the text. The reference cantilever and the requirement for flexibility are only loosely specified, so many observed depths can be reconciled with the claim. The data support a descriptive comparison and do not cleanly establish the functional reason.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare vertebral depth-to-span ratios of large vertebrates with the depth an engineering cantilever of similar load would use, and test whether shallower columns are more flexible under the same material. A large, consistent shortfall in depth together with a flexibility gain would support the claim; depths inside the engineering range, or no link between depth and flexibility, would undermine it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
What an engineer would build depends on the allowable stress, safety factor and load case, none of which Thompson fixes.

Shallow spines also follow development and phylogeny, so flexibility is hard to isolate as the reason.
